title: Marching into the Duma: The cost of Putin’s push for war veterans in parliament – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Sixty Ukraine-war veterans entered Russia's 450-seat Duma in 2026 under Putin's 'Time of Heroes' scheme, but polling-station forensics show veterans enjoyed no electoral advantage and their seats required sharply more direct fraud, with the 'clean' core of stations falling from 70% to 32% in veteran-contested constituencies. The author concludes the veterans project carries political costs, narrows space for future moderation, and leaves the regime more exposed to sudden unrest.

insights.claim: When Russia's new 450-seat Duma convened on September 30th 2026, 60 of the new deputies had fought in Ukraine, brought in under Vladimir Putin's 'Time of Heroes' scheme to move veterans into government.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Russia is institutionalising a war-linked political class, which matters for the durability of its war policy.
insights.quote: he was one of the 60 new deputies who had fought in Ukraine.

insights.claim: United Russia increased its Duma seats from 324 in 2021 to 349 in the 2026 election.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: The ruling party's enlarged majority gives the Kremlin unchallenged legislative control during wartime.
insights.quote: United Russia, the ruling party, which increased its seats from 324 in 2021 to 349.

insights.claim: The Kremlin likely treats military service in Ukraine as proof of loyalty and is using veterans to build a recruitment pool for future appointments, as with Alexander Shuvaev, who served briefly as deputy governor of Irkutsk before becoming governor of Belgorod in May.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Veterans moving into regional governorships signals a slow militarisation of Russia's administrative elite.
insights.locator: For Putin, the value of this pool

insights.claim: War veterans sit on 28 of the Russian Duma's 34 committees but chair only two, making committees a training ground for future appointments.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Veterans are being seeded broadly but not yet given real power, implying a multi-year elite-renewal plan.
insights.quote: veterans sit on 28 of its 34 committees, but they chair only two.
insights.locator: For Putin, the value of this pool

insights.claim: Almost 40% of Russians expect returning war veterans to bring more conflict and crime, and veterans report repeated job rejections once employers learn of their war service.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Veteran reintegration is a latent social-stability risk inside Russia that could fuel crime and discontent.
insights.quote: Almost 40% expect veterans’ return to bring more conflict and crime

insights.claim: Of the 56 United Russia veterans who entered the Duma, 31 won single-member constituencies with an average vote share equal to or slightly below United Russia's party-list share in the same constituency.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Official results contradict Putin's claim of 'broad support' for veterans, suggesting weak genuine public enthusiasm for the war.

insights.claim: In a 1:3 matched comparison, United Russia veteran candidates averaged 47.6% of the vote versus 47.1% for comparable non-veteran United Russia candidates, showing no meaningful veteran advantage.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: War service is not a vote-winner in Russia, undermining the Kremlin narrative of popular war support.
insights.quote: Mean vote shares were 47.6% for veteran candidates and 47.1% for the matched comparison group.

insights.claim: None of the 25 war-veteran candidates fielded by Russian parties other than United Russia in single-member constituencies won a seat in the 2026 Duma election.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Without administrative support, veterans lose, a clear signal of limited organic popularity for the war cohort.
insights.quote: none of the 25 veteran candidates these parties fielded in single-member constituencies won a seat.
insights.locator: Results for veterans standing for parties

insights.claim: Reading beneath official results, Russian voters appear less keen on ex-soldiers in parliament, challenging the Kremlin's portrayal that its electoral majorities reflect broad willingness to bear further costs of war.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Headline Russian election results overstate societal support for war, relevant to assessing escalation capacity.

insights.claim: Russian researchers detect direct electoral fraud by plotting turnout against vote share across polling stations: clean stations form a single-peaked cluster, while ballot stuffing stretches it into a 'comet's tail', allowing a 'clean' core to be identified.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Polling-station forensics provide a quantitative tool to gauge true public sentiment in authoritarian states.
insights.quote: direct fraud increases both recorded turnout and the beneficiary’s vote share, stretching the main cluster into a “comet’s tail”.

insights.claim: Nationwide, only about 18,500 Russian polling stations (21.3%) were classified as relatively clean in 2026, compared with roughly 43,000 (45.2%) in 2021.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: The 2026 Duma election was Russia's most heavily rigged parliamentary vote, indicating growing regime reliance on coercion over consent.
insights.quote: in 2026, only around 18,500 stations (21.3%) were classified as relatively clean, compared with roughly 43,000 (45.2%) in 2021.

insights.claim: In the 29 single-member constituencies contested by war veterans, the 'clean' core of polling stations fell from 70% to 32% between 2021 and 2026, a steeper drop than the fall from 61% to 29% in the other 182 constituencies.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Installing veterans required extra fraud, a measurable political cost of the Kremlin's war-elite project.
insights.quote: Across the 29 such constituencies we compared, the “clean” core fell from 70% to 32% against 61% to 29% in the other 182 constituencies.

insights.claim: In a Komi constituency, the Communist incumbent Oleg Mikhailov narrowly led veteran Stanislav Kochev 32% to 31% among 'clean' polling stations, yet the official result gave Kochev a 42% to 24% victory.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: A concrete case of fraud overturning a likely opposition win shows the gap between official and real Russian sentiment.
insights.quote: Within the “clean” core, Mikhailov narrowly led Kochev by 32% to 31%. Yet, the official result gave Kochev a decisive victory against Mikhailov, 42% to 24%.

insights.claim: The share of Komi's votes cast in 'clean' polling stations fell from around 94% in 2021 to just 61% in 2026, indicating a large expansion of direct fraud to secure a veteran's victory.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Fraud is spreading into previously clean regions, eroding the regime's remaining channels for gauging opinion.
insights.quote: the share of Komi’s votes cast in the “clean” core fell from around 94% in 2021 to just 61% in 2026.

insights.claim: Perhaps owing to Putin's overconfidence, veterans were not concentrated in Russia's 20 to 30 'electoral sultanates' with tight local control over results, so their candidacies spread fraud into regions where counting had previously been relatively clean.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Kremlin overconfidence is generating avoidable legitimacy costs across Russian regions.
insights.locator: Such stations have long been scarce

themes.theme: Implications for Europe and regime stability

insights.claim: A new wave of Russian mobilisation or aggression against EU countries could meet resistance from Russians reluctant to support the war, requiring more resources and coercion, though European governments cannot count on this to stop the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Domestic reluctance raises the cost of Russian escalation but does not remove the risk, so European defence spending needs remain intact.
insights.quote: Such costs should inform assessments of Russia’s capacity to escalate, but European governments can’t count on them to prevent the Kremlin from pursuing its ambitions.
insights.locator: What the results mean for Europe

insights.claim: Promoting people whose careers and legitimacy are tied to the war creates incentives to defend war policies, which may gradually narrow the space for moderation and make a future Kremlin change of course harder.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: A veteran-heavy elite lowers the odds of a durable Russia-West thaw, relevant to sanctions-relief and peace-deal scenarios.
insights.quote: Veterans’ advancement creates incentives to defend the policies that brought them into office, even when their promotion has limited electoral appeal.
insights.locator: Over time, promoting people whose careers

insights.claim: Wartime repression has suppressed but not resolved the kind of discontent that drove Russia's 2011 mass protests over electoral fraud, leaving the regime vulnerable to sudden unrest that, as in Iran, could be sparked by economic grievances.
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
insights.so_what: Europeans may need to price tail risk of sudden internal instability in Russia, not just external aggression.
insights.quote: So, as well as preparing for unpredictable Kremlin actions abroad, Europeans may need to plan for sudden instability within Russia too.
